newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown jittery, seen on long and slow decline.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown jittery, seen on long and slow decline.

text.p: The Czech crown's jittery performance on Wednesday could signal the beginning of a long and slow decline in the currency's fortunes although a sharp decline is unlikely, dealers said.

Just after trading began, the crown dropped by nearly 50 basis points against the midpoint of its mark/dollar basket to +3.2 percent after a local newspaper reported that several German banks expected the crown to weaken.

A few minutes later, the currency recovered slightly after the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) released results of a survey of local importers and exporters showing that most expected a trade deficit in the first quarter of 45 billion crowns ($1.6 billion) compared with just 27.1 billion in the same period in 1996.
Dealers acknowledged it was ironic that such a poor trade forecast was reassuring, but they said the crown's volatility still reflected general nervousness of a market grasping for signals.
"The market here is just nervous. The last 14 days have seen growing rumours about the Czech crown," said Jakub Perina of Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
"There is no strong background with economic fundamentals to make the crown stronger," he added.

Instead, the CSU forecasts further negative fundamentals. It predicted the overall 1997 trade deficit to rise to between 211 to 219 billion crowns to exceed last year's record shortfall of 160.3 billion crowns. Analysts said the crown will inevitably suffer from the expected record deficit later this year and wipe out its recent gains.

From about late December to early February, the crown gained roughly three percentage points over parity with the basket, spurred by nearly 40 billion crowns worth of crown denominated Eurobonds, issued because of relatively high Czech interest rates.
At the crown's peak earlier this month it rose to +5.5 percent over parity before talk about central bank intervention jolted the markets, forcing the currency below +4.0 percent.

"I think that there has been some feeling in the last 2 to 3 weeks, probably it's a little psychlogical..but the crown could go lower. We can't really expect (plus) four to five percent again (over parity)," said Tomas Becvar of Komercni Banka. "By the end of the first half of the year, we could go further with some depreciation."

The crown's recent decline has also been actively encouraged by the Czech National Bank, which has so far only tried to talk it lower by saying the wave of Eurobonds was irrational and that interest rate cuts were a possibility.
The central bank continued to follow the market, fixing the crown at 28.452 to the dollar after Tuesday's fixing at 28.345, and at 17.032 to the mark from 16.907.
The above rates imply a deviation from the midpoint of the central bank's mark/dollar basket of +3.47 percent, down from +4.05 on Tuesday.
The one year Prague InterBank Offered Rate (PRIBOR) stood at 11.23 percent on Wednesday.
